results.title: Nigeria’s health partnership with the US: National sovereignty and domestic financing By Muhammad Ali Pate, Nigeria's Coordinating Minister
results.description:
Nigeria’s health partnership with the US: National sovereignty and domestic financing

By Muhammad Ali Pate, Nigeria's  Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare 

_The destination is clear: a health system financed increasingly by Nigeria, governed through Nigerian institutions and able to sustain better outcomes for Nigerians._

For more than two decades, Nigeria and the United States have worked together on major public-health challenges. Through the US President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), the President’s Malaria Initiative, polio eradication, laboratory development, disease surveillance, health security, and contributions through the Global Fund and Gavi, that partnership has saved lives and strengthened institutions on which millions of Nigerians depend.

Nigeria values this record of cooperation, but the next phase must serve a clear national purpose. No country of our size can indefinitely finance essential health services through external assistance. Our responsibility is to preserve the gains built with partners, while expanding domestic financing, strengthening Nigerian institutions and ensuring that critical services remain available as the international financing environment changes.

*A National Framework for Transition*
That direction was established before the current bilateral arrangement. In December 2023, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu presciently launched the Nigeria Health Sector Renewal Investment Initiative and the Health Sector Renewal Compact, bringing the Federal Government, the 36 states, the Federal Capital Territory and development partners behind a common reform agenda. Through the Sector-Wide Approach, fragmentation and duplication are being reduced, while public and partner resources are, for the first time, being aligned behind one plan, one budget and one report, with clearer responsibility for results and a deliberate transition towards national ownership.

When the United States revised its global health approach in 2025 under the then new administration of President Donald Trump, its emphasis on country ownership, country systems, and government-to-government cooperation converged with reforms that Nigeria had already begun. The immediate task was to protect the continuity of treatment and prevent reversals in HIV, tuberculosis, malaria and other essential services, while strengthening the domestic foundations on which those services must ultimately rest.

The health MoU signed by Nigeria and the United States on 19 December 2025 was negotiated within that policy framework and should be understood in that context. Covering April 2026 to December 2030, it provides a managed transition from externally financed implementation towards stronger use of Nigerian institutions, government systems and domestic resources, while preserving essential services as Nigeria assumes a larger share of their financing and management.

*Financing the Transition* 
The financing structure under the MoU makes this purpose clear. The planned United States support is nearly $2 billion over five years and declines over the period, while Nigeria plans nearly $3 billion in additional domestic health financing. Nigeria’s contribution is not transferred to the United States; it remains in Nigeria and is applied to priorities determined by Nigeria, including HIV, tuberculosis, malaria, maternal and child health, laboratories, health workers, surveillance, commodities, primary healthcare and health information systems. There is no credible path out of aid dependency that does not require Nigeria to invest more of its own resources in the health of its people.

The Federal Government had already begun to translate this commitment into the budget. The 2025 federal health budget rose by nearly 60 per cent, increasing health’s share of the national budget to 5.2 per cent from just over 3 per cent. 
.....1/3

results.title: No. There is no credible evidence that USAID funded Boko Haram. In February 2025, US Congressman Scott Perry alleged USAID money went to gro
results.description:
No. There is no credible evidence that USAID funded Boko Haram.

In February 2025, US Congressman Scott Perry alleged USAID money went to groups including Boko Haram, without providing specific proof. The US Ambassador to Nigeria stated there is absolutely no evidence of such diversion, noting Boko Haram has been a designated Foreign Terrorist Organization since 2013 and that strict controls prevent aid from reaching terrorists. Nigerian probes into the claim have produced no verified findings. Boko Haram's known funding comes mainly from local crime, kidnappings, and other sources.
